text: A hot, very dry summer in Mendoza was followed by scattered rain and hail at the end of March, complicating the final weeks of harvest.
A mildew-hit spring worried growers, then sunny ripening weather and a cool, dry March produced healthy, deep-coloured Malbec and other reds.
A dry, very warm summer with a February heatwave still gave Mendoza healthy, ripe grapes, helped by the region's dry air and cool nights.
A dry spring with zonda wind stressed the vines, then light mid-March rain helped the grapes reach full ripeness; Malbec stood out.
A cooler, later year with frost and February hail, followed by 40 dry, warm autumn days that ripened the crop slowly.
A cool, dry season gave slow ripening and a late harvest, interrupted by one large December hailstorm that damaged part of the crop.
A hot, humid El Niño year with patchy hail and an early harvest; the INV described it as complicated but very good in the end.
Frost on 14 and 15 April struck most Mendoza vineyards before the harvest had finished, damaging fruit on vines still waiting to be picked.
A warm, very dry season with cold nights, plus some frost and hail, gave Mendoza a below-average crop of healthy grapes.
A cool, dry year in which spring frost trimmed Mendoza yields, and slow ripening through the cool autumn led to a late harvest.
A cool, damp season with a November frost slowed the vines, and the Mendoza harvest ran 14 to 20 days later than usual.
Frost and zonda wind cut the crop; a hot summer was followed by a cool March and a late harvest.
A cool, healthy year with hail in parts of eastern Mendoza; elsewhere the slow, cool season gave fresh, elegant wines.
Heat, frequent rain and hail cut the Mendoza crop, and the rain-diluted grapes gave wines that came in low in alcohol.
Heavy rain brought mildew and botrytis to Mendoza; vineyards on slopes, and growers who picked early, fared better than the rest.
A cool, very wet El Niño year brought hail and mildew that cut the Mendoza crop, but the slow, cool ripening gave fresher, lower-alcohol wines than usual.
A dry, frost-shortened year with a small crop and an early harvest that came in just ahead of April rain and hail.
A dry, sunny season with an early harvest and a Mendoza crop back to normal size after the small, weather-hit vintages of 2016 and 2017.
Heat, about half the usual rain, and spring frost and hail produced a small, early crop in Mendoza in the season before the pandemic harvest.
Frost, hail and February rain in a cool year with some mildew; the wines were fresh and lower in alcohol.
A dry spring with frost and hail cut the Mendoza crop, and some rain fell at harvest, though the fruit that remained was of high quality.
Frosts on 31 October and 1 November 2022, then historic drought and the hottest summer in decades, cut yields 25 to 30%; Mendoza picked about three weeks early.
Persistent wind, frost and a January heat spike, moderated by cool nights, gave low yields across Mendoza in 2024, though the fruit kept its freshness.
A record-early hot start brought rapid ripening, then February rain split the Mendoza vintage in two, separating early and late picks.
The earliest flowering on record, from 25 May to 8 June, then a very hot June to August; harvest began on 15 September, and early-October rain brought botrytis.
A cool spring, late flowering from 15 to 25 June and a cooler September slowed ripening; few noble sweet wines were made.
Rain of about 220 l/m² from 6 to 12 August brought the worst Danube flood in memory; many dry-stone terrace walls collapsed, though dry, warm weather afterwards ripened the grapes well.
Very early flowering and a very hot summer, then early-October rain prolonged the harvest, and snow on 24 October with minus 5°C interrupted picking.
A wet June, a dry summer, then cool, wet weather into October; harvest began only on 20 October, with significant yield losses, especially for Riesling.
About 300 l/m² of rain fell in July and August in the Wachau after normal flowering, but excellent October weather allowed a fine harvest.
Snow lasted until mid-March, then hot, dry June flowering caused coulure in Grüner Veltliner; a cool, wet August preceded an exceptional autumn.
An extremely mild winter and early budburst, a hot, dry July, then a wet September with 140 l/m² that delayed harvest into November.
Heavy June and July rain with very warm nights, then a cool, wet autumn delayed ripening; the harvest ended in early December.
High Danube water and June rain, July thunderstorms with mudslides, and a wet, warm September that brought heavy botrytis in Riesling.
Long snow cover, a very cold, rainy May and June coulure in Grüner Veltliner and Riesling led to very low quantities; harvest began only around 15 October.
Frost on 5 and 6 May damaged shoots in eastern sites, a late-August heatwave followed, and a dry, warm autumn brought no significant botrytis.
Winter fell to minus 20°C, a frost on 18 May hit some sites, and a dry summer led to an early harvest without botrytis.
A once-in-a-century Danube flood in early June, a June heatwave that caused coulure in Grüner Veltliner, and drought from July to mid-August stressed dry-farmed terraces.
Early growth after a warm March, then humid, warm August nights brought disease and a difficult harvest with yield shortfalls.
Record heat, with July the hottest month since measurements began, and severe drought until August; fungal pressure stayed low and botrytis was mostly limited to late-picked Riesling.
Late-April frosts devastated the Spitzer Graben, with losses up to 90%, and also hit Weissenkirchen and Arnsdorf; a wet summer followed.
One of the hottest summers on record with almost no rain caused drought stress until mid-August rain; Riesling yields were slightly lower.
On 21 June hail tore through the Spitzer Graben, causing major yield losses near Viessling and Gut am Steg, in an otherwise very hot, early year.
Early budbreak, May rain, then a very hot, extremely dry summer; Riesling ripened slowly on the terraces while Grüner Veltliner ripened quickly, and harvest began in mid-September.
Two late-March frost spells, then walnut-sized hail on 22 August struck Spitz, the Spitzer Graben, Rossatz, Arnsdorf, Mautern and Dürnstein.
Late budbreak and a dry spring, then frequent July and August rain with hail in Rossatz and Dürnstein-Loiben; a sunny, dry autumn allowed long hang time.
Mildew after a wet June cut Grüner Veltliner yields, July drought hit unirrigated sites, a wet September brought rot and October rain botrytised Riesling.
A hot, dry summer was interrupted by a hailstorm on 26 August that damaged grapes in several villages; picking ran from mid-September into early November.
April frost nights hit the Spitzer Graben, Weissenkirchen and Rossatz, a long summer heatwave followed, and heavy rain from 12 September halted picking for one to two weeks.
A cool, rainy July, then a late-October wet spell that brought early botrytis to Riesling while Grüner Veltliner stayed healthy.
Bushfires in the 2019 to 2020 summer burned vineyards in parts of the Adelaide Hills and smoke damaged fruit in others, while some areas were untouched; yields were well below average.
Poor flowering, hail, exceptional summer heat and rain at harvest combined to give South Australia a small crop, so Barossa growers had both low yields and weather-damaged fruit to sort.
A wet start was followed by prolonged hot, dry weather and rain just before the March harvest, with some sunburned fruit.
Poor weather at flowering cut yields, and an unusually cool summer led to a late, slow harvest of fresh, balanced fruit.
A drought season with dry, hot conditions kept yields down in the Barossa, the fourth in a run of dry years.
Extreme heat just before harvest trimmed the crop, yet Australia still crushed a record volume after a dry, warm, stable season.
A large crop of very ripe fruit came in after a warm season, and Barossa growers had ample, fully ripe grapes to work with.
Rain interrupted the harvest at the end of the fourth drought-affected season in a row, so picking dates were critical.
Drought and spring frost gave a very early, very small harvest; Barossa vines set few bunches of small, thick-skinned berries, and national yields per acre were the lowest since 1976.
An early start and then a record March heatwave in the middle of the Barossa harvest, followed by some rain; very ripe fruit had to be brought in fast.
Another heatwave year with drought and a smaller crop: a long summer heatwave hit South Australia during ripening and scorched exposed Barossa fruit.
Good rain finally broke a long drought in South Australia, and later rain brought some mildew to the Barossa's vineyards in an otherwise favourable season.
A wet, cool season across most of Australia brought heavy botrytis and downy mildew pressure to the Barossa, and strict selection decided quality.
High winds and drought, plus poor bud fruitfulness carried over from the wet 2011 season, lowered Barossa yields and gave small crops of concentrated fruit.
The hottest summer on record for south-eastern Australia reduced yields and ripened many varieties quickly and at the same time.
Frost, high winds and heatwaves all lowered Barossa yields in 2014, and a deluge of rain in February interrupted the season before harvest.
A warm summer and an early harvest in South Australia; bushfires in the nearby Adelaide Hills raised concerns about smoke taint.
A dry, early season with heat spikes brought one of the earliest South Australian harvests on record, mostly finished by mid-February after a warm summer gave full ripeness.
A cool, wet start brought disease pressure and a later harvest than 2016, but dry weather during picking helped quality.
Early frosts reduced Barossa yields, then consistent weather in the second half of the season supported quality in the fruit that remained.
Spring frosts sharply reduced yields in South Australia, and severe bushfires burned through undergrowth dried out by the summer sun.
Growing-season rain about 50% below average in a cool, dry year cut Barossa yields by 60 to 70%; Grenache and Riesling were the standouts.
Below-average temperatures all season and good rainfall gave close-to-average Barossa crops after two tiny drought harvests, and the cool weather allowed an unhurried pick.
A cool season with hail in central Barossa in late October and in the north in late February, plus spring frost; harvest ran about two weeks late, into May.
La Niña brought a wet October and over 150 mm of rain in November against an average near 35 mm, then downy mildew and botrytis pressure; valley-floor picking ran into May.
A dry winter and spring brought budburst about three weeks early, then September and October frosts badly damaged some vineyards and cut yields.
A second dry year, possibly the driest on record from August to harvest, with two severe late-September frosts; picking began in January and most fruit was in by the end of March.
Repeated October frosts, up to about 30 separate events in some vineyards, cost Coonawarra about three-quarters of its crop in a drought year.
A cool, short ripening season; old vines on shallow terra rossa gave clean, ripe fruit early, but quantities were small.
The season started about three weeks late, frost struck and cool, humid flowering caused poor set; yields were very low, similar to 2002.

About 117 mm fell from 18 to 26 January just before picking, and 150 mm in the first fortnight of February. Whites were mostly in by late January; reds ripened through the wet until it cleared after mid-February.
Rain fell through the white harvest and regularly through February and early March, and much red fruit was left unharvested.

Drought, only 15 mm of rain from October to December and January heat over 35°C on 12 days were followed by smoke from the bushfires. Smoke taint destroyed the Shiraz and other reds; only a token amount of rosé was made.
Pokolbin recorded its wettest year on record in 2022, 1,365 mm over 97 rain days, so downy mildew was a constant threat; harvest started late and yields were low.
A warmer, drier season than average pushed reds two to three weeks early, and the harvest finished by the third week of March, about four weeks ahead of normal.
A wet winter, on-and-off January rain and a wet March demanded constant vigilance against disease; Chardonnay and Cabernet were picked about two weeks later than usual.
November rainfall about double the average and significant rain in early February, just as harvest began, raised disease pressure in warm, humid weather; the crop was about 32,000 tonnes.
The driest and warmest growing season on record, with very little spring rain and none through to March; disease pressure was negligible and the harvest early.
In Australia's lowest-yielding vintage per acre since 1976, drought and frost hit South Australia and some McLaren Vale estates saw total yields fall by about a third.
Patchy frost, a drawn-out fruit set and a short, severe heat spike left Shiraz and Cabernet yields at all-time lows, while Grenache was near normal.
A dry, warm season brought budburst, flowering, veraison and harvest earlier than ever before; some producers picked from late January.
A late-January heatwave reaching 45°C cut yields about 30%, then the Black Saturday fires of 7 February burned about 154 ha of Yarra vineyards. Smoke returned on 13 February and badly tainted Shiraz.
Smoke from the Hunter and then Gippsland fires drifted over the valley, though taint tests came back negative; yields were very low after a hot November and erratic temperatures.
Spring rain and difficult flowering weather cut yields 30 to 40% below average, and a cool, dry run-in to a late harvest gave Chardonnay of high natural acidity.
The wettest August and October on record and a La Niña spring wet until Christmas drove heavy downy mildew and significant crop losses, before a dry, sunny summer.
Widespread spring frost caused crop losses of up to 70% in parts of Chile, sharply reducing the 2014 harvest in the worst-hit vineyards.
El Niño brought unusual rain to Rapel, Maipo and Colchagua, hitting the reds at harvest; national yields fell about 25%.
Three days of sub-zero temperatures in October 2019, worst in Colchagua, followed by summer heat and water shortage cut national yields about 13%.
A frost-free season with only isolated heat spikes, yet Colchagua yields fell up to 30% on 2024, especially Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Carmenère.

A wet El Niño winter, with 438 mm in Puente Alto against 178 mm the year before, and a cool spring delayed ripening by one to ten days; Maipo logged 1,722 degree days against a ten-year average of 1,810.
The earthquake of 27 February 2010 struck Maule and Curicó weeks before harvest; the growing season itself was cool and late.
In January 2017 wildfires burned through the Maule and O'Higgins regions, damaging more than 100 vineyards; wineries elsewhere sorted grapes for smoke taint.
An extremely warm season brought forest fires to southern Maule and Biobío, rapid ripening, and yields about 20% below 2022.
An exceedingly hot summer ripened a small crop to very high sugar, and botrytis followed. The Thanisch estate's Bernkasteler Doctor became the first Trockenbeerenauslese ever made in the Mosel.
An exceptionally warm, sunny season followed by botrytis made 1959 the gold-standard benchmark for ripe, sweet Mosel Riesling, and later vintages such as 1971 were measured against it.
Rain during flowering, then botrytis in a fine autumn, produced what were regarded as the best Mosel wines since 1959.
The hottest summer in a century brought drought and low yields, then autumn botrytis made legendary sweet wines, including Trockenbeerenauslese.
Heat near 40°C, botrytis and low yields produced a small, concentrated Mosel crop, regarded as the finest since 1971, after a perfect autumn across Germany.
September rains compromised grape health and spread rot through the Mosel, so the earliest-picked grapes made the best wines of the year.
A damp but cool September preserved acidity and a warm, sunny October boosted ripeness, giving small yields of Riesling with plentiful botrytis.
A warm summer was followed by rain before the October harvest, so few Mosel wines rose above Auslese level in a year of uneven ripeness.
A scorching, dry summer stressed Riesling and gave a smaller, uneven Mosel crop, with heat stress and drought the defining problems of the year.
A poor summer was rescued by a sunny autumn, and yields were relatively high; the Mosel made fresh, aromatic Riesling from a late harvest.
Quantities were low, but noble rot developed rapidly in the autumn, especially in the Saar, giving the Mosel plenty of botrytised Riesling to work with.
Summer and autumn rain, then rampant rot at the end of September forced Mosel growers to pick early and select hard to keep their Riesling clean.
A hot April brought record-early flowering, then a very cool summer and a fine autumn extended ripening, giving long hang time and a dry harvest.
Very late ripening in cool autumn temperatures meant few botrytis wines in the Mosel, but growers who waited made a reasonable crop of Eiswein.
A dry, warm, reliable growing season gave ripe, fruity Mosel wines with healthy grapes, though German volume was about 12% below 2008.
Low sunshine and high rainfall devastated yields, though an extremely hot July and excellent autumn botrytis gave tiny volumes of concentrated, very high-acid wine.
A warm spring and a golden September brought a very early, uneven Mosel harvest with high yields of ripe Riesling after a generally warm season.
A cool, wet summer with poor fruit set cost the Mosel up to 25% of its crop, before a warm, dry September and October rescued ripeness.
Late flowering and hail, then a damp, warm October with harvest rain and botrytis, cut the Mosel crop by more than a quarter.
A season that was too cold and too wet left Mosel growers fighting rot, although yields were higher than in the small 2013 vintage.
A hot, dry summer followed by a cool, golden October gave ripe Riesling with high acidity, and botrytis developed late in the season.
High rainfall in early summer brought heavy disease pressure in the Mosel, along with late frost and hail, before weather improved from July.
Spring frost after an early budburst cut the crop, and midsummer rain raised disease pressure. The small harvest came early, and careful selection was needed to bring in healthy Riesling.
A hot, dry year gave a bumper crop of healthy grapes and an early harvest, though some fruit was left hanging in the heat too long and acidity was mild.
Extreme summer heat caused sunburn and a smaller crop; two rainy August weeks helped, and harvest finished before late-September rain.
A warm, sunny spring and a hot, dry summer brought an early, healthy harvest from late August, with growers picking in the cool early mornings.
A cool, wet spring and rain from June to September brought high disease pressure and small crops; July floods devastated the nearby Ahr valley, and late-December cold allowed some Eiswein.
A hot, very dry year with low disease pressure and Sahara-like conditions into September; yields were about 2% above the long-term average.
The warmest year on record in Germany: a hot, dry June, then a wet August that caused rot, rescued by a dry September.
April frost and large May hailstorms cut the Mosel's crop to about 510,000 hl, 30% below 2023 and the smallest in 50 years, in a wet, mildew-prone season.
Heavy mid-September rain and smaller berries with low must yields cut volumes in much of Germany, with Rheinhessen down 23%, but the Mosel's yields came in above average.

A July heatwave above 36°C and drought from late July into September gave a very early harvest, Müller-Thurgau from about 20 August, and a crop about 10% above average. Acidification was approved early because of high pH.
Late frost cut crops in eastern Germany by up to 70%, but the Pfalz was largely spared and its 2024 crop slipped only about 4%, to around 2.2 million hl.

Record March warmth pushed budburst early, then April frost hit the lower slopes along the Rhine, at one Lorch site for the first time in a century. Downy mildew pressure was so high that Schloss Vollrads sprayed 13 times.
Small berries and low must yields, then heavy mid-September rain; the Rheingau, like the Pfalz, recorded a double-digit fall in volume while the Mosel came in above average.
Drought left the Marco de Jerez with a particularly short harvest of about 44.4 million kg of grapes, and dry conditions persisted into the following season.

Rain of 425 to 480 l/m² against a normal 600 kept the crop small at 49.9 million kg; June hail struck Trebujena and Lebrija, and August heat and levante wind cut coastal yields. Albariza soils held moisture well.
A wetter spring and a mild summer with frequent dew and few levante days let the crop recover to 62.5 million kg, up 25% on 2023, though rainfall was still below average.
A late-June heatwave scorched grapes and damaged Cariñena vines, then severe drought produced extremely low yields, and slow ripening dragged the Priorat harvest into early October.
A wet winter and spring brought downy mildew and major crop losses, then a dry summer led to one of the earliest harvests on record.
Extended drought stressed old vines, especially in the southern villages; a very hot season gave an early, short harvest with very low yields.
Good subsoil water, then severe winter and spring frosts delayed the cycle; pleasant weather from veraison and large day-night swings aided ripening.
A hot March brought early budbreak, there was no frost or hail, and a warm, dry summer caused few dehydration problems.
A dry winter left groundwater almost exhausted; warm weather from veraison stressed vines on light soils until late-September rain helped them finish.
A cold, wet year with anomalous cold from 15 May to 15 June delayed the cycle; a cold September and cloudy October brought botrytis.
A mild, dry winter brought early budbreak, then a cooler spring and good set; late-August heat aided ripening, and harvest ended before late-September rain.
A dry, hot summer naturally limited yields, and the harvest came slightly early with no rain during the final ripening.
Ribera del Duero harvested about 133 million kg of grapes in 2016, the largest crop of the decade to 2025 and the baseline against which the 2017 frost losses were measured.

Frost on the night of 27 to 28 April held temperatures below 0°C for over seven hours, down to about minus 6°C. With only about 250 mm of rain, the harvest fell to 55 million kg, 58.5% below 2016, picked from 8 September.
After the 2017 frost, Ribera del Duero's crop more than doubled in 2018, up 127% to about 125 million kg, a full recovery in a single season.
Low groundwater and a mild but extremely dry summer caused water stress; some vines stopped ripening while others waited for full maturity.
Rain during the growing season and at harvest brought mildew pressure, and picking was postponed several times while growers waited for dry spells.
A January snowstorm, then frost and storms in late May and early June, fungal disease and a two-week summer heatwave reduced yields; September rain complicated picking.
A very hot growing season with almost no rain caused uneven ripening and small berries, and growers had flexibility over harvest timing.
Early-season and summer drought were followed by scorching late-August heat in Ribera del Duero, and early-September rain had little effect before a warm October.
Spring frosts cut the crop to about 95.5 million kg after four years above 105 million; September rain both helped and complicated picking, which ran to 4 November.
No frost or hail, but extreme drought from spring and late-season heat gave small berries. The crop rebounded 36% to about 129.6 million kg, picked from 28 August to 28 October.
A warm season with some heat spikes and a little harvest rain still delivered healthy grapes with excellent analytical balance, and the Consejo Regulador rated the vintage Excelente.
A cool, late year with hail, mildew and harvest rain was saved by a long, fine harvest period that let growers pick at full ripeness.
A dry, healthy year: low disease pressure and a generous crop of sound grapes, despite some rain at harvest, led the Consejo Regulador to rate 2005 Excelente.
Spring rain, hail and mildew, then a dry August and September heat spike, followed by harvest rain; the Consejo rated the vintage Muy Buena.
A season of hail, mildew and harvest rain, rescued by a dry, sunny autumn that allowed a selective, drawn-out harvest.
A wet spring and cool summer with mildew cut yields, but a long Indian summer saved the vintage and let late grapes ripen.
A hot, dry summer with May hail and September rain; the early harvest of ripe grapes was rated Muy Buena by the Consejo.
Stable weather through the season and moderate yields gave balanced, healthy grapes, and Rioja's Consejo Regulador awarded its first Excelente rating since 2005, repeated the next year.
Drought and a small crop of very healthy grapes led the Consejo Regulador to rate the vintage Excelente for the second year running.
Drought kept Rioja yields low through the summer, until late-September rain helped the grapes finish ripening in a small but sound harvest of concentrated fruit.
Mildew, botrytis and a wet harvest produced a heterogeneous Rioja vintage in which picking dates and strict sorting decided the quality of the wine.
A warm, dry year brought what was then Rioja's earliest harvest on record, a record broken again two years later; the Consejo rated it Muy Buena.
Drought and summer heat, then a favourable autumn allowed a two-month selective harvest of healthy grapes across Rioja, giving growers time to pick each plot at its peak.
Spring frost and a hot, dry season gave Rioja a small crop, and the harvest was the earliest on record in the region.
A wet spring brought mildew, stormy early July brought hail, and a long harvest followed a season that produced a large crop.
A stable, healthy season with a smaller crop of balanced grapes earned Rioja its first Excelente rating from the Consejo Regulador since 2011.
A rainy spring brought local mildew, but the season finished in balance, and the Consejo Regulador rated the vintage Muy Buena.
April frost and June hail struck Rioja in a dry season, trimming the crop in affected vineyards, but the surviving grapes ripened well and the Consejo rated the vintage Muy Buena.
Rioja's hottest year on record, with heat spikes, drought and hail; the small berries stayed healthy and were picked early, and the Consejo rated the vintage Muy Buena.
A dry start and late-August heat were followed by heavy September rain that brought botrytis, so quality varied with picking dates.
Low fruit set, mildew and botrytis, then harvest rain after a dry, warm summer; the Consejo Regulador rated the vintage Buena.

A heavy mildew attack, hail and poor fruit set after the September 2024 rains, plus subsidised green harvesting, made 2025 one of the shortest crops in Rioja's history, below the 260 million kg recorded in 2024.
The earliest flowering on record and a favourable season, then some rot in late August and heavy October rain; late-harvest wines were made.
Cold weather at flowering, a coolish summer and a wet September were rescued by late autumn warmth that favoured late-picked wines.
An exceptionally cold winter, good flowering weather that set a large crop needing thinning, then early-October rain that threatened some grapes before the late pickings.
The heatwave produced very low acidity, and Alsace growers were permitted to add acid, rare for the region. Harvest was early and the wines broad.
Quite a bit of rain fell during the season, and growers had to manage rot pressure to bring in healthy grapes.
Alsace picked healthy, ripe grapes in a very early harvest, even earlier than in the heatwave year of 2003, after a season that ran well ahead of the usual calendar.
Challenging weather throughout the season held ripening back, and Alsace wines came in with high acidity and a lean, firm structure after a cool year.
Chaotic weather through the 2010 season cut Alsace yields about 20% below the previous year's level, leaving growers with a small crop to work with.
Average volumes, a warm, steady August and a cool, dry September left Alsace vineyards disease-free at harvest, so growers could pick clean, ripe grapes at leisure.
A stop-start season gave a very small Alsace crop, and harvest rain spread rot, so growers who picked early generally fared best.
A cool August preserved high acidity in Alsace whites, but botrytis was weak and the late-harvest wines were disappointing compared with drier styles.
A gloomy June gave way to a scorching summer and a very early September harvest; the small, healthy crop allowed late-harvest sweet wines but acidity was lower than usual.
Alsace avoided hail and frost and had good yields; a wet June raised mildew risk, then a warm, dry rest of the summer led to a good, healthy harvest.
Spring frosts cut yields by up to a third in places, but a warm summer with enough rain and good harvest weather followed.
A wet first half of the season was followed by a sunny, hot summer that gave good ripeness, though the heat softened Riesling's acidity.
A mild winter, a cool spring, a warm summer with enough rain and a cool, dry September allowed a long harvest window.
Spring frosts and a wet May to July with mildew cut production about 20% below normal; a sunny, dry autumn followed, but very few sweet wines were made.
A very warm, dry year with intense heatwaves and an early harvest; conditions were poor for botrytis and grey rot appeared once rain arrived.
Alsace escaped the southern heatwaves; two weeks of rain in early August replenished the vines, and Hugel reported not a single speck of botrytis, so no late-harvest wines were made.
Mildew and a humid, disrupted flowering cut Alsace's crop by about 13% in a very wet French vintage, a lighter loss than in Burgundy, the Loire or Champagne.

Alsace opened its harvest on 19 August, three days earlier than the previous record set in 2018 and 20 to 25 days earlier than normal. June heat and an August heatwave pushed sugars up about 2 degrees of potential alcohol a week.
A hot, dry summer drove the Loire river to record low levels in August; mid-August rain saved Anjou and Touraine from serious drought damage.
Rain during the picking period made the 2002 Beaujolais harvest difficult, and sorting out damaged Gamay bunches decided the quality of the wines.
An extremely dry season stressed the vines in the European heatwave year, and Beaujolais harvested a small crop of very ripe Gamay.
A hot, dry year brought water stress to Beaujolais vineyards, but the Gamay grapes still reached full phenolic ripeness at harvest.
Alternating climate extremes gave way to a better end to the season; southern Beaujolais was more consistent than the north.
A lack of sunshine and mildew problems hampered ripening in Beaujolais, and the crus fared better than the regional Beaujolais wines.
A rainy year with widespread hailstorms, rot and mildew made 2008 a difficult Beaujolais vintage, with yields cut and sorting essential.
Beaujolais brought in its smallest harvest in 40 years, about 509,000 hl, or roughly 30 hl/ha across the region, in a year of short crops throughout Burgundy as well.
A cool, moist spring and early summer delayed flowering to mid-June, and the harvest ran late, from the end of September into October.
A warm spring and early flowering, a cool summer and a hot, dry September allowed a harvest in ideal conditions.
A sunny, dry spring with ideal flowering, then a warm to hot summer with heat spikes offset by rain and cool nights; harvest began on 24 August.
Three hailstorms on 13 April, 27 May and 24 June battered the northern crus; the last two affected about 1,500 and 2,250 ha. The southern Beaujolais' ample crop offset some of the losses.
Hailstorms on 10 and 31 July struck Beaujolais-Villages and the crus; some Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent growers lost up to 80% of their grapes.
A very wet, mild winter, then a hot, dry, sunny summer with August the hottest since 1959; harvest began in late August.
Severe early-April frosts cut the crop, July heat passed 40°C and late-August hail hit the south. Production was about 400,000 hl, roughly half of 2018.
Hot, very dry July and August caused drought and sunburn in sandy parcels, and a very early harvest began around 20 August.
Savage April frosts, a cold May, June hail and a cold, wet July; veraison came 18 days behind 2020, and harvest began in mid-September.
Late-June hail, then a hot, dry summer that cut the crop by a third on 2021. Picking began on 17 August, the earliest on record apart from 2003.
Budbreak around 7 April without frost, the hottest June since 2003 and 2017, and an early-September harvest; volumes rose about 20% on 2022.
A very wet spring and early summer brought heavy mildew and black rot, and late-June hail followed. After a hot, dry August, a cool, wet September slowed ripening and rewarded growers who waited.
Heatwave, mildew, coulure and hail combined to give Beaujolais its lowest yield in at least 35 years, about 32% below the small 2024 crop.

A severe frost on 2 May, after a hard winter freeze, slashed the crop. A hot, drought-stricken summer with peaks near 37°C in July and September then concentrated the survivors; picking began on 13 September, yielding tiny volumes of very dense wine.

One of the hottest and driest seasons on record in Bordeaux, yet the vines still carried a large crop. Heat and drought pushed the grapes to a ripeness rarely seen at the time, giving rich, ripe, supple wines.
Cold, wet weather at flowering cut the potential crop, then a hot, dry summer ripened the reduced load fully, completing a trio of warm post-war vintages with 1945 and 1947.
The hottest and driest year of the decade: drought held yields down and the grapes reached high sugar ripeness, giving rich, ripe, supple wines.

Frost at the end of May struck after an early, even flowering, then August was extremely hot and dry. Picking began on 22 September and some leading estates harvested only about 11 hl/ha, which explains the wines' rarity and concentration.
Near-ideal summer heat and a warm, dry Indian summer brought in a record crop of very ripe, healthy grapes, an unusual pairing of size and ripeness for Bordeaux at the time.
A cold, damp spring gave way to a fine summer and then a record-dry September, which let growers pick ripe, healthy fruit without pressure. The dry finish rescued an uncertain season.
The hottest summer since 1949 drove the earliest Bordeaux harvest since 1893. Heat and drought gave very ripe grapes and supple, generous wines.
A second hot year running, with the hottest and driest summer in decades. Heat and drought gave very ripe grapes on both banks and rich, supple wines.

The worst frost since 1945 burned young shoots across Bordeaux in spring, and a cool season followed. Many estates harvested a fraction of a normal crop, and 1991 became a byword for scarcity and difficult ripening.
A wet spring brought an early mildew scare, then a warm, dry summer and settled harvest weather delivered healthy, fully ripe grapes on both banks, and some harvest rain did little harm.
A soaked winter, a patchy summer and a cool, late harvest gave reds of moderate ripeness, while the same damp autumn made 2001 a standout year for Sauternes.
Wet weather at flowering caused coulure and millerandage, and a cool summer followed. A dry, sunny September rescued ripeness, but the crop was small and the wines classically firm.
An unprecedented August heatwave, with drought, forced a very early harvest. Some vines shut down under heat stress, so soil water reserves and picking dates decided quality more than usual.
A wet August worried growers, but a sunny September ripened a big, late crop. Careful thinning and patient picking produced classically proportioned Bordeaux.

An exceptionally dry, warm year without damaging heat spikes. Water stress kept berries small and thick-skinned, and an unhurried harvest in fine weather brought deeply coloured, structured wines on both banks.
A hot July was followed by a cool August and storms in mid-September, which forced a hurried harvest as rot threatened, and botrytis appeared in the sweet-wine zone.
A cool, damp summer brought heavy mildew pressure and uneven ripening. A dry, sunny September and October saved the vintage, giving lighter, early-drinking reds and fine dry whites.
Spring frost and a wet, cool spring cut yields, then a dry July and a sunny autumn allowed a late harvest of ripe fruit. The crop was small, and the wines fresher than the cold start suggested.
A warm, sunny summer with cool nights and a dry harvest period ripened both Merlot and Cabernet fully. The wines were ripe and powerful, with high natural sugar and generous fruit across the region.
A dry, sunny summer without scorching heat kept berries small, and cool nights preserved acidity. The result was high tannin and alcohol balanced by freshness on both banks.
Early heat and dryness pushed the season well ahead, then a cool, damp summer slowed it. September sunshine rescued the harvest, but uneven ripening made sorting essential.

A soaked spring, a hot, dry August and then autumn rain shaped the year. Early-ripening Merlot was picked before the worst of the rain, so the Right Bank generally fared better than late Cabernet on the Left Bank.

A cold, wet spring caused poor flowering, then harvest-time rain spread rot. The smallest Bordeaux crop since 1991 was picked in a rush, and strict sorting was needed to make light, early-drinking reds.

A cool, damp summer left the crop behind, then a hot, dry September and warm October delivered a late rescue. The long, sunny finish gave fresh, well-structured wines from a crop that had looked compromised in August.
A hot, dry June and July built ripeness early, and August rain refreshed the vines. The harvest was unhurried and healthy, producing ripe, generous reds with supple tannins.
A very wet first half filled the soils, then a bone-dry summer followed. The late harvest brought in a large, healthy crop with ripe tannin and freshness.
Frost in late April cut the Bordeaux crop by about 40% overall. Vineyards that escaped went on through a normal season, with some September rain, and made fresh, fruity reds.

A wet, warm spring brought a severe downy mildew attack and some hail, then three dry, sunny months followed. Growers who kept the mildew at bay picked ripe, concentrated grapes in a stress-free harvest.
A long, dry summer included a July heat record, and some rain at harvest. Balanced, ripe reds and fresh whites came from a season that never quite tipped into excess.
A wet spring was followed by about 54 days of summer drought, an early harvest and a reduced crop. Small, concentrated berries gave dense reds, and the vintage was made under pandemic conditions.
April frost, a very wet June with heavy mildew, and a cool summer gave a small, late crop. The wines were lighter and fresher than recent warm years, with lower alcohol and bright acidity.

Record heat and drought, after spring frost and hail in places, kept berries tiny. Bordeaux made about 411 million litres at roughly 38 hl/ha, and the small, healthy grapes gave surprisingly fresh, balanced reds.

A warm, humid June unleashed downy mildew: about 90% of Bordeaux vineyards were affected to some degree. Merlot suffered most, with some estates expecting 40% losses, before a dry, sunny late summer ripened the survivors.
A relentlessly wet year brought frost, hail, mildew, poor flowering and harvest rain. Bordeaux made about 332 million litres at roughly 35 hl/ha, a tiny crop of fresh, fruity, lower-alcohol wines.

Hot and dry from May to August: 2025, 2022 and 2003 had more days above 35°C than any other year this century. Dry whites were picked in August, and the crop, at 33.6 hl/ha and 290.6 million litres, was the smallest since 1991.

Late frosts in early May destroyed part of the crop, and a long, hot summer with timely rain followed. Picking started in late August, one of the earliest dates in Burgundy's history, from a small, concentrated harvest.
Early flowering, then a long, hot, dry summer refreshed by September rain. Yields were record-setting and the grapes very ripe, an uncommon pairing of quantity and quality.

A cold, wet spring lasted to the end of June and held back flowering, so the crop was modest. A warm, sunny August and September then ripened it, and the late harvest brought in uniformly healthy grapes.

A brutally cold January and a slow spring delayed the season, then warm summer weather and a sunny September ripened grapes evenly. Picking began around 24 September with generous Pinot Noir yields and very healthy fruit.
A warm winter, cool spring and then a long, hot summer, refreshed by rain in August and September. Berries were small and highly concentrated, and severe frosts were avoided.

Early flowering and a wet July, then mid-September rain fell mainly south of Beaune. The Côte de Nuits was largely spared and made attractive reds, while Côte de Beaune reds suffered more from the rain.
A cool, wet year with a damaging hailstorm on 2 August and some harvest rain. The Côte de Nuits generally outshone the Côte de Beaune.
A dry, warm summer was followed by a cool north wind in September that dried and concentrated the grapes. Healthy, balanced fruit gave classic reds and whites with both ripeness and acidity.
April frost reduced the crop, then the August heatwave peaked around 42°C. Picking started in mid-August from a small harvest, and many grapes had raisined on the vine.
A cool summer with hail damage was saved by a clear, sunny September. Acidity stayed high, and the whites were generally more successful than the reds.
A very dry, often grey summer kept the grapes healthy and small, and fine September weather ripened them fully. The reds combined ripeness, concentration and fresh acidity.
A wet spring, record July heat, then a cool, wet August with hail and rot pressure; warmer September weather rescued the harvest, but sorting was essential.
A cool, rainy summer with mildew and rot was saved by a sunny September; the reds were fragrant and light, and yields were reduced by sorting.
A cool, damp, hail-affected season left rot pressure high until a north wind in September dried the grapes. The crop was small and acidity high.
A cold winter, mid-July storms and then hot, dry weather brought a healthy, unhurried harvest of very ripe Pinot Noir, giving rich, generous reds.
A severe winter freeze damaged vines, then a rainy flowering caused coulure and a damp summer followed. A cool, dry September saved a crop up to a third below average.
A very warm early spring pushed the vines ahead, then a wet, stormy summer with July hail and rot pressure followed; picking began in late August.
Frost, hail and a cold, wet flowering slashed the crop, and mildew followed. A hot, dry August then ripened what was left into concentrated wines.
A cold start delayed the season, poor flowering cut the crop and July hail added to the losses. The small crop was picked late, after a cool year had held ripening back.
June hail struck the Côte de Beaune again, then a sunny September ripened healthy, fresh grapes and saved what had looked a difficult year.
A hot, dry and early year: extreme heat and drought briefly shut some vines down, and picking began around 27 August. The small crop of thick-skinned berries gave deeply coloured, ripe reds.
A hard late-April frost, followed by hail and mildew, cut yields everywhere, in some villages drastically. A warm, dry summer then ripened the surviving grapes.
Frost struck the north of the region, but the Côte d'Or went on through a hot, dry spring and summer to an early, plentiful and very healthy harvest.
A wet winter recharged soils, then a hot, dry summer produced a large, healthy crop picked from late August. The reds were ripe and generous.
April frost and cool flowering trimmed the crop, then a very hot, dry summer with several heatwaves cut yields further. Small berries gave concentrated wines that still kept surprising freshness.
A mild winter and a hot, dry summer with minimal disease brought a record-early harvest. Yields were low, but the grapes were ripe and kept surprising freshness.

Hard frost in early April hit buds already out after a warm March, then a wet, cool spring brought mildew and harvest rain. Only early-September sunshine let the tiny crop ripen; the wines are light and fresh.
Spring frost, four heatwaves and summer drought, yet the vines carried generous yields. The early harvest gave ripe, healthy grapes and a welcome return to normal volumes after 2021.
Storms, local hail and harvest heat did not stop Burgundy bringing in its largest harvest on record, about 1.9 million hectolitres according to the BIVB, with no lasting heat stress on the vines.
An extremely wet season with frost, hail and severe downy mildew. Losses reached up to 80% for reds in the north of the region, and only a dry August allowed the survivors to ripen.

Heatwaves in June and August pushed the Côte d'Or to one of its earliest harvests, with some estates picking from 19 August. A ten-day August heatwave concentrated sugars fast; yields were small, around 30 hl/ha for reds at some estates.
Spring frost struck the north of Burgundy, including Chablis, after an early budburst; a hot, dry spring and summer followed and the harvest was early and healthy.
In April 2021 night temperatures fell to about minus 7°C in Chablis, and some estates lost up to 95% of their potential crop, one of the worst frosts in the appellation's modern history.

A June heatwave during flowering caused coulure and millerandage, then August heat accelerated ripening. Picking began around 28 August, and early-September rain complicated the end of harvest; yields ran 35 to 50 hl/ha.
Spring frost cut the crop, then a hot, dry summer concentrated what remained. The small harvest of very ripe grapes made 1921 one of the legendary Champagne vintages.
Record sunshine, heat and drought, the same conditions that shaped Bordeaux's famous 1947, produced very ripe, rich, low-acid grapes in Champagne, an unusual style for the region at the time.
The hottest European summer on record to that point brought drought and an early harvest of very ripe, soft grapes.
A brutal winter freeze and spring frost damaged vines across Champagne and cut yields, then a cool season produced a small crop of precise, high-acid wines.
A see-saw season ended with grapes showing both unusually high sugar and unusually high acidity, the combination that made 1996 one of Champagne's most famous vintages.
Hail, a stormy July, mildew and rot pressure made a difficult first half, and a warm August rescued ripening; the result was a sound but modest Champagne vintage.
A season without extremes: steady ripening brought in healthy, balanced grapes, and 2002 became one of the most celebrated Champagne vintages of the decade.
Spring frost destroyed much of the crop, and then the record August heatwave and drought shrank the rest. The tiny harvest gave opulent, low-acid wines.
A cool August gave way to an Indian summer, and the vines carried a record yield of healthy grapes, with elegant, pure wines.
Mildew pressure marked the season, and the grapes came in with high sugar and low acidity, giving rich, forward Champagnes best drunk young.
A cool, wet summer with mildew and botrytis pressure gave precise, high-acid wines in which Chardonnay generally outshone the Pinots.
A cool, grey season was rescued by a dry September; the grapes were healthy and the wines notably fresh and saline, a classic long-ageing vintage.
A hot, dry August with heat spikes and some mildew produced rich, ripe, plush Champagnes, generous in style and suited to earlier drinking than cooler years.
Frost, hail, rain and mildew cut the crop sharply in spring and early summer, then a dry, hot late summer ripened a small crop of very healthy grapes.
A cold, wet spring with hail, mildew and later botrytis delayed the season; a record-sunny summer helped, but harvest began in October, very late by modern standards.
A dry spring gave way to a cool, wet summer with mildew, before a sunny September ripened a large crop of high-acid grapes.
Unprecedented heat and drought lasted into mid-August, and picking began on 29 August, giving an early, healthy crop with the broad, ripe profile of a hot year.
Frost, record spring rain, mildew, hail and botrytis cut the Champagne crop by at least 30%, though careful growers still brought in healthy grapes.
Frost destroyed about 23% of buds in April, then a hot early summer and late-August storms brought rot. The harvest was early, and sorting was essential.
After a record-wet winter came the hottest summer on record in Champagne, with drought and local hail. The big, healthy crop was picked early in fine conditions.
Spring frost, two summer heatwaves, drought and some mildew trimmed the crop, but cool nights during ripening kept the grapes fresh and aromatic.

Record drought and heat brought Champagne an early harvest from 17 August, two weeks ahead of the long-term average. Yields were capped at 8,000 kg/ha because of the Covid sales slump, more than 25% below 2018.
Spring frost, hail, persistent rain, mildew and botrytis made 2021 one of Champagne's hardest recent years, with a tiny crop.
A dry summer with well-timed rain kept the vines working without disease pressure, and Champagne brought in healthy grapes with its largest yields since 2008.
A record number of bunches, then heat spikes and humid weather brought uneven ripening and botrytis in a huge crop.

Frost on 22 to 25 April damaged about 9% of the crop, mostly in the Côte des Bar; May hail took about 70% of the potential on 500 ha of the Marne valley; and downy mildew reached the bunches on 95% of monitored plots.

Temperatures above 25°C from late April and 30 to 35°C in mid-June drove a very early harvest: first picks on 19 August and appellation-wide from the week of 25 August. Hail on 3 May destroyed 245 ha; mildew stayed low and quality was high.
A hot summer finally broke a run of four rain-plagued vintages, 1991 to 1994, in the southern Rhône, after years in which Grenache had struggled to ripen.
Early budburst and flowering, then a warm season with on-and-off rain and more near the end of harvest; most Grenache ripened fully before the late rain.
A wet season until mid to late summer, then a strong mistral in late August and warm, sunny August and September weather dried and ripened the grapes.
Heavy rain and flooding swept much of the southern Rhône in 2002, swelling and rotting grapes before harvest and leaving Châteauneuf with a small, difficult crop.
Relentless heat and drought made 2003 an extreme year in Châteauneuf, with very high sugars, low acidity and shrivelled berries.
A cool, moist spring and strong June mistrals that disrupted flowering led to a late season in Châteauneuf, with slower ripening than in recent years.
Warm, dry, sunny days and cool to cold nights over a long growing season let Grenache ripen slowly while keeping freshness and structure.
A cold winter with January frost, strong summer mistrals and then rain during harvest made picking dates important in Châteauneuf.
One of the driest years on record, with early, even flowering and more than two weeks of mistral in late August and early September. The wind kept the grapes healthy and concentrated.
A wet, rainy year with difficult conditions from start to finish in Châteauneuf. Disease pressure stayed high through the season, and sorting was essential.
Hot, dry, sunny weather with timely rain and strong mistrals gave very ripe, healthy grapes and powerful wines in Châteauneuf.
Grenache coulure and a very dry summer cut yields, and the wines showed riper tannins and more freshness than the warmer 2009 vintage.
A warm, dry spring, a cool July and then a long Indian summer with a heat spike ripened a normal-sized crop.
A dry, sunny season with patchy drought and a small, uneven crop; Grenache fared better than Mourvèdre after August rain.
A cold spring caused severe coulure in Grenache, cutting the crop sharply, and the harvest was late. The wines were lighter and fresher than usual for Châteauneuf.
A rainy winter, a cool summer and a wet September made for slightly lighter southern reds, with dilution a risk for growers who picked too soon.
A long, hot, dry season gave ripe, powerful reds across the southern Rhône, with neighbouring Gigondas especially successful alongside Châteauneuf.
A very hot, very dry summer with cool nights and late rains just before a long harvest gave fresh, firm, balanced reds.
Coulure on Grenache and a dry, warm season gave an early, small crop, with low yields at many estates and ripe, healthy grapes.
Torrential spring rain and the most humid conditions since 1973, without the drying mistral, unleashed downy mildew. Yields fell sharply, though the summer turned hot and dry.
A sweltering, very dry year across the southern Rhône, where Châteauneuf-du-Pape produced the most successful wines of the vintage despite the drought.
Harvest volumes varied widely across the southern Rhône after a dry, warm season, and the Châteauneuf reds came out supple and balanced.
The April frost reached the southern Rhône and a cooler season followed, giving fresh, fruity wines with lower alcohol than recent vintages.
Drought and hail marked the 2022 season in the southern Rhône, and the harvest came early. Despite the stress, Inter Rhône judged the southern reds excellent.
A dry winter, a wet spring and then a long, healthy harvest gave finely structured, balanced Châteauneuf wines with moderate ripeness.
A wet, mildew-hit start, spring frost and Grenache coulure cut yields, followed by heat later in summer. The small crop gave fresh, balanced wines with moderate alcohol.
Heatwaves and smaller crops marked the southern Rhône season, yet early tastings found the Châteauneuf wines fresh and balanced despite the heat.
In April 2021 some Côte-Rôtie estates lost their entire crop to frost, and Inter Rhône's president feared the smallest Rhône harvest in 40 years.
Hail and mildew struck in a wet first half; hail cut the Hermitage crop, before a warm, very dry August and September ripened the rest.

Left Bank yields fell sharply in the hot, dry 2025 season: Saint-Julien was about 37% below its 2005 to 2024 average, Margaux 29%, Pauillac 27% and Saint-Estèphe 17%. Small berries promised concentrated, tannic Cabernet.
Spring frost devastated Muscadet's yields and a cold, wet early summer followed across the Loire, where Sauvignon Blanc yields in the centre were also lower than usual.
Frosts on 26 to 27 April, then catastrophic May and June mildew, gave Muscadet its smallest crop since 1949; about a third of the zone went unpicked.
Mildew and poor fruit set halved Muscadet's yields in a very wet season that cut Loire production by about 30%.

Pomerol's yields were about 31% below average in the hot, dry 2025 season, while neighbouring Saint-Emilion lost about 10%. Drought stress on younger vines and few bunches after the difficult 2024 flowering explain the shortfall.
A July hailstorm devastated Quincy, Reuilly and the Coteaux du Giennois in an otherwise excellent year, and also trimmed yields in Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé.
Merlot on Saint-Emilion's clay and limestone ripened before the autumn rain set in, giving the Right Bank an edge in a year when late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon struggled more.

Merlot, the backbone of the Right Bank, was the variety hit hardest by the 2023 mildew outbreak, while Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon proved more resistant. Yields varied hugely from estate to estate.
Late rain caused rot in Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, so growers had to sort hard, while further west late warmth in Anjou aided the sweet Chenin wines.
A hot, dry year with drought-reduced yields across the Loire, but cool nights kept the Sauvignon Blanc grapes fresh and aromatic despite the dry summer.
Delayed flowering and autumn rain diluted Cabernet Franc and halved Muscadet yields, but Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé fared well, free of rot.
A wet June and August brought mildew pressure across the Loire, but Sancerre fared well while Anjou, Saumur and Touraine struggled.
Mid-July hail hit Sancerre in a year of April frost in the central Loire, valley-wide mildew and October wind and rain from Hurricane Kirk.
April frosts reduced Sauternes and Barsac to a tiny crop in the worst Bordeaux frost year since 1945, leaving very little fruit for the autumn botrytis harvest.
Heavy rain set in after the red harvest and prevented botrytis from developing cleanly in Sauternes, turning a promising Bordeaux year into a very difficult one for sweet wine.
After a soaked winter and patchy summer, autumn rain followed by warm days encouraged extensive botrytis. Sauternes and Barsac picked richly concentrated grapes, a standout sweet-wine year.
A cool, small vintage across Bordeaux; botrytis developed mainly in vineyards near the rivers, giving Sauternes a small crop after a wet flowering.
An extremely hot, dry season left little humidity for noble rot, so Sauternes saw only limited botrytis and grapes concentrated largely through heat.
A very difficult year for Sauternes, with uneven botrytis and rain, so strict selection was needed to make good sweet wine.
After a dry, warm summer, autumn brought plentiful noble rot, letting Sauternes and Barsac estates pick concentrated, evenly botrytised grapes in a generous year for sweet wine.
Mid-September storms in Bordeaux brought rot pressure rather than clean noble rot, and botrytis influence in Sauternes was limited that year.
A cool, damp summer was followed by a dry, sunny September and October; precise picking and selection gave fine Sauternes.
April frost devastated Sauternes yields. The fruit that survived developed good botrytis during a sunny autumn, so the sweet wines were fine in quality but tiny in quantity.
Heat and humidity arrived at the right moment in autumn, spreading rich botrytis through Sauternes and Barsac in a warm, sunny Bordeaux vintage.
A dry, sunny summer was followed by late, irregular botrytis, so Sauternes harvesters had to make many passes through the vines to pick nobly rotten berries.
Autumn rain made 2012 a difficult year for Sauternes; Barsac had slightly better conditions than Sauternes itself, and selection was severe.
Uneven autumn weather and harvest rain gave extremely low yields in Sauternes, in the year of Bordeaux's smallest overall crop since 1991, and only strict selection produced sweet wine.
Botrytis set in during September and returned in force in late October, giving Sauternes two waves of noble rot after a cool summer.
Botrytis spread evenly and quickly between late autumn showers, so Sauternes estates could pick concentrated, clean noble-rot grapes after a hot, dry Bordeaux summer.
A very dry summer delayed noble rot until late in the season, and some fruit was picked before it arrived.
Late-April frosts reduced Sauternes yields, and noble rot developed unevenly in autumn, so quality depended on careful, repeated passes through the vines.
Hail and downy mildew reduced the Sauternes crop, and a hot, dry summer and autumn gave little chance for serious noble rot to form.
A very hot, dry summer was followed by rain in late September and early October, which set off botrytis and gave Sauternes a late crop of noble-rot grapes.
Yields were very low and noble rot came late after a cool, rainy October, leaving Sauternes estates a short picking window in mid-October.
Spring frost and summer hail cut the crop, but a damp autumn encouraged good noble rot on the grapes that survived, giving a small Sauternes vintage.
The hot, dry season held back botrytis until rain in late September; Sauternes harvesting then ran to the end of October.
A near-tropical spring brought downy mildew to the Sauternes vineyards, then a warm, sunny August; white grapes in the area were harvested from late August.
A wet season with downy mildew, coulure and millerandage reduced the Sauternes crop well before autumn, leaving little fruit for the botrytis harvest.
April frosts hit the Loire hard: Muscadet yields were 35 to 40% below normal and Saumur-Champigny about 30% down, while Savennières lost up to 95% at some estates.
A June hailstorm all but wiped out the crop in Vouvray and Montlouis, in a cool year that also left many Loire reds short of ripeness.

In the week of 30 August, hail and wind damaged about 4,600 ha of vineyards in Kvareli, Telavi and Gurjaani just before the rtveli harvest; the state paid growers per hectare and bought damaged grapes.
Hail, heavy rain and wind struck Kakheti during the harvest, affecting more than 3,500 ha in Telavi, Sighnaghi, Kvareli and Gurjaani; the state bought about 1,050 tonnes of damaged grapes.
Georgia processed about 336,000 tonnes of grapes in the 2025 rtveli, a record for the last 30 years, with Kakheti supplying about 327,000 tonnes.

After three consecutive years of drought, Santorini expected only 350 to 400 tonnes of grapes, its worst harvest in living memory, against 2,500 to 3,000 tonnes a year over the past decade and up to 5,000 in 2003.
An early, warm year; early-September rain and morning fogs spread fine botrytis over ripe grapes, and a dry Indian summer then shrivelled them into excellent aszú berries.
An unusually warm year with a harvest stretching from August to mid-November; October rain triggered botrytis on very ripe grapes and Aszú was made.
A very rainy year: botrytis came with heavy grey rot, and humidity stopped the berries drying. Only meticulous selection on well-drained loess produced decent wine.
A late, rainy spring was followed by heat until September; a colder, wetter September brought intense botrytis and a dry spell then concentrated the aszú berries.
The hottest and driest year to date in Tokaj: most producers made no Aszú, and only October rain brought late botrytis to a few select plots.
A mild spring with early budburst, a cool April and May, then summer heatwaves alternating with rainstorms; heavy botrytis on very ripe grapes made 2017 one of Tokaj's great Aszú vintages.
A washout year: botrytis developed alongside heavy grey rot, and the air was too humid for berries to dry, so fine Aszú was scarce.
An extremely hot, dry season held back botrytis; where it did arrive, humid autumns stopped drying, and some estates made szamorodni instead of Aszú.

Record rainfall of about 59 inches for the year, 33.5 inches of it in the growing season, left little sound fruit for drying. Bertani skipped Amarone Classico, Amarone was made in small quantities and most selezione and riserva bottlings were not made.
A warm, dry season with intermittent rain and long, stress-free ripening, but hail cost some Valpolicella estates up to 25% of their crop; big day-night swings thickened skins for drying.
Drought and above-average temperatures from May to July required emergency irrigation; dry, breezy autumn weather then suited appassimento, though the heat sped it up.
Persistent rain peaking in July brought local hail and constant mildew pressure, so less fruit was set aside for Amarone than for Valpolicella.
A rainy spring led to heavy June mildew, mid-August hail struck the Classico zone, and heavy September and October rain followed; fewer grapes were selected for drying.
A cold, wet summer with heavy mildew pressure, though Barbaresco largely escaped the September hail that ruined much of Barolo.
A cool, damp summer with high disease pressure kept growers spraying, but Barbaresco largely escaped the July storms and hail that struck parts of Barolo, mostly hitting Dolcetto.
A spring hailstorm struck both Barolo and Barbaresco in 1986, and production in both zones was very modest, leaving only small quantities of wine from the year.
A warm, early year in Piedmont gave ripe, generous Nebbiolo, and both Barolo and Barbaresco harvested early in fine conditions after a hot summer.
A wet winter and May, then a dry, very hot June to October with large day-night swings and only two brief storms; healthy grapes were picked at a normal date.

After a very wet May and a humid, stormy summer with heavy downy mildew, a devastating September hailstorm struck the heart of the Barolo zone. Yields fell 40 to 50%, and Michele Chiarlo made no crus at all.
About four months of drought and heat, with highs near 40°C, brought the earliest Piedmont harvest in two centuries, Moscato from 16 August. Yields fell about 40%.
About 450 mm of spring rain refilled soils after the 2003 drought, then ideal dry summer weather with wide day-night swings; harvest ran from 8 September to 16 October.
A warm, fairly dry summer turned wet at the end: about 110 mm of heavy rain fell on 9 to 14 October, after most Barolo Nebbiolo had been picked by 8 October. Yields were 10 to 18% below 2004.
A long, cold winter, a late, rainy spring, then a dry, warm summer with rain in late August and on 20 September; vigorous natural yields needed thinning.
Growth ran about 20 days early after a mild winter; a cool, wet week at bloom reduced set, and Moscato was picked from 19 August.
A cold, wet June and early July with near-daily rain disrupted flowering and brought downy mildew. Sunshine returned in mid-July, and yields ended 15 to 20% below normal.
Early budbreak in March, a wet April and May, and August peaks of 32 to 33°C; harvest was brought forward, Nebbiolo picked by 30 September.
Heavy winter snow and rain, budbreak about ten days late and a dry May and June; Nebbiolo was picked by 6 October, at the traditional time.
A cool, dull July and a hot August caused drought stress in early September until storms of 25 to 35 mm; harvest came about two weeks early, yields about 10% lower.
A winter freeze near minus 20°C and about a metre of snow in February, then a hot, dry summer. About 80 mm of rain on 1 to 3 September saved the crop; yields fell 10 to 25%.
A cold winter and spring delayed growth by 15 to 18 days, and Barolo was picked as late as 22 October, the latest harvest in 20 years.

Warm spells in March and June gave way to a cool, cloudy, wet July and August that demanded frequent spraying. An August hailstorm damaged Barolo vineyards, though netted rows were spared, and yields were dramatically reduced.
Ample winter and spring rain, then no rain from mid-June to 10 August with frequent days above 30°C; mid-August rain helped, and Barolo was picked by early October.
A cold, wet late winter delayed growth by at least ten days; heavy spring rain was followed by dry ripening with only sporadic storms, and Barolo was picked by mid-October.
Four nights of April frost damaged vines, especially in the Monferrato, then a hot, dry summer followed. The Langhe harvested about 10 days early with below-average yields.
February brought minus 10°C and 60 to 70 cm of snow; spring rain of 350 to 380 mm and over 950 mm for the year raised mildew risk, before an early-August heat peak near 35°C.
Heavy autumn rain built reserves, then a wet April and May, a hot, dry spell and heavy early-July rain; Barolo was picked as late as 18 October.
A mild winter and a wet May to late June slowed growth; veraison came in early to mid-August and Nebbiolo ripened from late September to early October.
Two nights of early-April frost damaged buds, hitting about 30% of production mainly in the Monferrato; a long, dry summer followed and Barolo picking began around 6 October.
Extreme drought and heat, with 30 to 32°C already in May and only about 120 mm of rain in Barolo in June and July. Harvest ran 10 to 15 days early, and yields were lower.
A mild, wet spring was followed by intense July and August heat, and hail cut yields hard in parts of the zone, especially La Morra.

More than 900 mm of rain fell over the year, with wet weather from February to May and again from mid-September. Disease control and thinning were decisive, and alternating rain and dry spells made picking dates tricky.
Two heatwaves reaching 37 to 38°C and a dry season brought an early harvest, from Moscato on 21 August to Barolo on 4 October, with yields slightly below average.
A wet spring brought mildew across Tuscany, and in August a hailstorm struck Montalcino, reducing yields. The surviving grapes ripened well but gave lighter wines than usual.
A wet season with fruit fly attacks made selection critical, and Biondi-Santi announced it would make no Brunello from 2014.
June mildew, then a hot, dry August, brought an early Tuscan harvest of very ripe Sangiovese, giving soft, round wines.
April frosts reduced the crop, a dry June and July followed, and a wet August and September threatened vine health near harvest.
An exceptionally wet summer caused rot across Tuscany, and many grapes failed to ripen fully before harvest, so strict selection was needed to make sound wine.
The hottest summer in 150 years, with April frost and drought, brought the earliest Tuscan harvest since 1945. Only the highest Chianti Classico vineyards escaped heatwave conditions.
A cold winter and rainy spring were followed by a warm summer and a hot October; the Tuscan harvest ran 15 to 20 days later than usual.
A cold winter, a cool, wet August in Chianti Classico and rain in September made for a late, difficult harvest across the zone.
A wet spring, a very hot July and a sunny early September ripened Sangiovese well across Chianti Classico and Montalcino after a demanding start to the season.
A mild, dry winter, record spring heat and a hot July pushed Tuscany to an early harvest, with yields down about 10%.
A very wet winter, a hot May reaching 30°C, about 30 days of rain from mid-May, then August days up to 40°C; cooler sites gave the best results.
A very wet winter and spring and a cool season left ripening about 15 days behind; July heat helped, and Sangiovese was picked as late as the third week of October.
A very cold, snowy winter and a hot April, then record heat in mid-August; some growers picked at the end of August, and September stayed very warm.
A very cold, snowy February, a warm, dry June and a hot July and August stressed the vines until late-August rain revived growth and ripening.
A very cool, wet spring delayed budbreak by about two weeks and May was very wet, but a near-perfect July to September brought a harvest in early October.
A cool, protracted season with frequent July and August hail and widespread downy mildew; a mild, dry September and early October saved much of the crop, and Tuscan yields fell about 20%.
A cold, rainy winter and irregular spring were followed by an exceptionally hot, dry summer, small bunches, reduced yields and violent August hailstorms in places.
A cool, wet spring, a hot, dry summer and September rain made up the Tuscan season, with drought stress and hail in places.
Late spring frost, very little rain from May and heat spikes in July and August cut Chianti Classico's output to about 206,000 hl, down 27% and the lowest production in 40 years.
A warm year in Tuscany, though less extreme than elsewhere in Europe; after the frost- and drought-hit 2017, yields returned to average.
A cold, dry winter, delayed budbreak, a very wet May and a warm June were followed by hailstorms in July and August and stable weather through harvest.
A dry winter brought early budbreak in late March, then freezing temperatures cut yields at lower elevations, and August heat reduced the crop further.
Frosts on 7, 8 and 15 April reduced yields, then a warm, dry May sped flowering and a hot, dry summer followed.
Extreme drought brought irregular growth and low yields in Chianti Classico, until rain in late August and early September saved the vintage and refreshed the vines before harvest.
Heavy rain in late spring and early summer unleashed downy mildew in Tuscany, followed later in the summer by violent hailstorms, and crops were smaller across the region.
Rain, hail and heatwaves alternated through the Tuscan summer, and a cool, wet autumn then slowed ripening, giving lighter Chianti Classico at lower alcohol than recent warm years.
Heat spikes, hail and spring frost cut the Tuscan crop in 2025, though early reports on the quality of the Sangiovese were positive.
A cold, rainy growing season pushed the harvest to 25 October to about 10 November, and yields were smaller; north-slope vineyards did best.
February snow at altitude, a May frost and late flowering cost 20 to 25% of the crop, and a late-June heat spike reached 40°C.
Little winter snow and a very dry, hot season left vines water-stressed; some estates used emergency irrigation and picked earlier than ever before.
Summer heat peaks added to the mildew damage, and the Etna consortium later reported that the 2023 crop had fallen by about 42.5%.
Heavy rain and humidity in May and June brought Etna's worst downy mildew in a decade or more. North-slope estates lost 70 to 95% in places, while the east side was largely spared.
Sicily suffered severe drought, but Etna's old mountain vines drew on deep reserves and late-August rain helped; the crop rose about 60% on 2023 to around 80,000 quintals.
Severe spring frosts decimated the Central Otago crop in 2004, a reminder of the frost risk in New Zealand's most continental wine region.
Central Otago had its coolest growing season on record, slowing Pinot Noir ripening, while New Zealand's national harvest reached about 457,000 tonnes.
The only New Zealand region whose crop grew in 2021, up 21% on 2020, while the national harvest fell about 19%.
December to February rain was only 44.4 mm, 37% of normal, in one of the driest and warmest seasons in years; frost was minimal and yields beat estimates.
A very late, deep frost early in the season and then a short, severe drought, though a late surge in berry weight held losses under 10%.
Rain-caused rot lowered New Zealand's yields at harvest in 2000, and Marlborough's Sauvignon Blanc vineyards shared in the losses that year.
Spring frosts across New Zealand cut the 2003 national harvest about 35% below 2002, with Marlborough's young Sauvignon Blanc industry sharing in the losses.
Widespread rot hit Marlborough at harvest time, so careful selection in the vineyard and well-judged picking dates decided quality in a difficult year for Sauvignon Blanc.
New Zealand yields fell to about 75% of average in 2010, and Marlborough's Sauvignon Blanc crop was correspondingly smaller than in recent years.
A warm, wet season brought fungal infection and a short ripening window across New Zealand, putting Marlborough growers under pressure at harvest.
One of the coolest New Zealand growing seasons on record, with national yields about 18% below normal and a late Marlborough harvest.
Early frosts cut yields for many New Zealand growers, though the season ripened grapes slightly better than the cool 2012 vintage.
Marlborough brought in its largest vintage ever after a warm season with good flowering, swelling Sauvignon Blanc supplies after small crops in 2012 and 2013.
A very dry summer cut Marlborough yields by about 20 to 25%, tightening Sauvignon Blanc supply after New Zealand's record 2014 crop.
A wetter, cooler season than usual and a late harvest cut New Zealand's volume about 9% below 2016, with rot pressure in Marlborough.
A warm summer pushed ripening ahead, then heavy rain at harvest brought widespread rot to Marlborough, forcing growers to pick quickly and sort hard.
A cool spring, late frosts and poor flowering weather in a third drought year cut New Zealand's harvest about 19%, to roughly 370,000 tonnes; Marlborough fell more than 20%.
A cool spring and a wet summer brought disease pressure, yet New Zealand's crop rose to about 532,000 tonnes, a rebound after the small 2021 harvest.
Poor fruit set cut Marlborough yields, but loose bunches resisted humidity and disease, and the South Island came through the cyclone season relatively unscathed.
A dry, warm season produced a small crop: Marlborough harvested 312,812 tonnes, 21% below 2023, while Central Otago's harvest slipped only about 4%.
A cooler summer and excellent flowering gave high, possibly record yields; growers thinned fruit, and rain on 18 and 19 March interrupted a slow Sauvignon Blanc harvest.
Heat and hailstorms marked a difficult Douro season, and Tinta Barroca was the main Port variety hit hardest by the storms.
A very wet winter caused erosion on the terraces, followed by a very hot July, and yields were higher than in 2008 and 2009.
Drought, compounded by hail, cut Douro yields by up to 40% in 2012, leaving water-stressed vines carrying only a small, concentrated crop at harvest time.
An uneventful growing season ended with a very rainy September that disrupted the harvest and cut both yields and quality; only a few houses released small amounts of Vintage Port.
Early-year rain damaged vineyards, a cool August followed and disease pressure was high, so Vintage Port declarations were most unlikely.
Drought gave way to heavy spring rain that eroded terraces, then a hot summer; yields were low across the Douro.
Early budbreak, heatwaves and the hottest July on record gave a small crop; late-August rain helped, and several houses declared Vintage Port.
Early budbreak, a dry, mild season and cool harvest nights gave healthy but below-average yields, with only some rain at harvest.
Hail, mildew, a summer heat spike and rain at harvest made for a demanding Douro season, and quality depended heavily on site and picking date.

A three-month drought left a 35% rain deficit, and an early-August heatwave held above 40°C for ten straight days, longer than in 2003. Yields fell about 30%, up to 50% for some whites, one of the smallest Douro crops in 40 years.
Oidium (powdery mildew) reached Madeira in 1851 and devastated the vineyards, the start of the island's long nineteenth-century wine crisis.
Phylloxera was identified on Madeira in 1872, arriving barely two decades after oidium and dealing a second blow to the island's vineyards.

On 20 February torrential rain on saturated ground sent floods and mudslides through Funchal and Ribeira Brava, killing at least 42 people. Cellars in Funchal flooded and stocks of old wine were likely lost.
Wildfires from about 8 August burned into Funchal, destroying buildings and forcing evacuations; producers reported the vineyards themselves largely safe at the time.
The post-war 1945 declaration ended the long gap after 1934, a pause in general declarations that was only approached again by the seven years between 2017 and 2024.
Nearly every shipper declared. A warm summer with no rain from June, light mid-September showers that swelled the grapes, high yields and fine harvest weather with cool nights.
An exceptionally wet winter was followed by a hot, dry summer; Pinhão twice recorded 45°C in August, but deep ground water prevented raisining. Rain fell at harvest and yields were well down.

Cool flowering cut yields, and picking began around 20 September in extreme heat that raisined part of the crop. 1970 was a general declaration and the last vintage bottled in the UK as well as Portugal.
Widely declared by every major shipper except Cockburn, Martinez and Noval. A wet winter and cool, overcast August were rescued by late-September heat.
Universally declared: a wet winter and cool spring, then fine weather from June and ideal harvest conditions with midday heat near 32°C.
