A wet winter ended three years of drought, heavy May rain checked the crop size, and most growers picked from about 20 September in fine weather; a major declaration followed.
Widely declared. A cold, dry winter delayed budburst, spring rain caused coulure, and a warm, dry summer ripened a small crop.
A very wet winter and cool spring were followed by a June heatwave that cut the crop; a long, late harvest ran into October with rain at the end.
A dry winter, spring and summer ended with heavy September rain that wiped out many crops; only early-picked fruit in the Douro Superior escaped the damage.

Extreme heat in late July and early August, with 45°C days, shut some vines down before early-September rain brought relief. Yields were very small and concentrated, and the vintage was widely declared.
The threat of rain at harvest forced early picking decisions; 2004 was not widely declared, and houses released single-quinta Vintage Ports instead.
An exceptionally dry season and very early harvest; resilient vineyards gave small, concentrated yields, and some producers declared while others made single-quinta wines.
Steady rain from November to February, then a dry August and September and mild temperatures allowed slow ripening without raisining. Second most widely declared vintage to that date.
A dry, cool season with some early picking; Quinta do Noval declared a Vintage Port, but 2008 was not universally declared by the major houses.
A very dry season that started early after a warm spring, then extreme summer heat and water stress reduced yields; some top producers declared, but not all.
Universally declared: a rainy winter, a warm spring with patchy mildew and hail, summer heat spikes and drought, eased by rain in late August and early September.
A dry spring and early summer, then one of the hottest Junes on record cut yields; some houses declared, while the two largest groups waited for 2016.
A wet, cold spring, a scorching dry summer and a rainy September; leading houses declared, the start of an unusual back-to-back pair with 2017.

A very dry, very hot year with spring and early-summer heatwaves and short summer storms; the harvest was the earliest on record. Yields were sharply reduced, and it became the most widely declared Port vintage to date.
A dry winter and spring, a cooler summer and late-summer rain gave near-average yields; there was no general declaration, but many single-quinta Ports were released.

Pinhão had about 70% less rain than normal from November 2021 to August 2022 and reached 47°C in July, Portugal's highest recorded temperature. There was no general declaration, but several houses released single-quinta Vintage Ports.

An exceptionally wet winter filled the soils, and a warm summer without scorching heat ended in near-perfect harvest weather from early September. Symington declared nine wines in the first general declaration since 2017.
A wet July left Chenin Blanc short of the ripeness needed for moelleux sweet styles, and Loire yields were slightly below average after a difficult summer.
The hot, atypical season pushed Sancerre and other Sauvignon Blanc to around 14% alcohol, and Chenin Blanc saw little botrytis.
A July heatwave was followed by cold, wet weather in August that brought rot pressure at harvest, so selection was decisive in the Loire.
A cool, wet summer brought rot that required careful selection, before a dry, warm September helped the remaining Loire grapes to ripen.
Late-September rain caused rot in Cabernet Franc, though late sunshine helped ripening; sweet Coteaux du Layon fared better than Vouvray in the conditions.
Fungal disease blighted the crop in Muscadet and Touraine in a warm, uneven year, and growers lost fruit to rot before and during harvest.
A warm, dry summer gave low yields in Touraine, and late-harvest rain caused some rot in Muscadet, in an otherwise ripe, healthy Loire year.
After a wet May and early June with some mildew, the Loire had its hottest summer since 2003 and driest since 1945. Quantity was good, with the heat ending the mildew threat.
Five frost episodes between 4 April and 6 May hit Muscadet and Anjou hardest, while Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé were largely spared. Cold, rainy flowering then caused coulure.
A warm, wet winter and a very warm spring, with June hail in Reuilly, Menetou-Salon and Châteaumeillant, and a hot August.
Severe April frosts caused losses of 70 to 90% in many Muscadet and Anjou vineyards and touched every zone including Sancerre; a cold, wet June and July with mildew followed.
Drought stress affected some areas and young vines, but cool nights and low disease pressure helped, and the Loire harvest came very early.
A violent hailstorm on 1 June devastated parts of the Mâconnais; some vineyards lost 80% or more of their crop, and one estate averaged only about 15 hl/ha.
A wet, cool spring caused coulure that cut yields across the northern Rhône, then a late, healthy harvest delivered fresh, structured Syrah with clear expression of each site.
A fine late August was followed by early-September rain that diluted a large crop; the reds were soft and fruity and the whites full-bodied.
A wet, mildew-prone start kept northern Rhône growers spraying, then a warm, dry finish arrived and the Syrah ripened late but cleanly.
A small crop with low yields after a cool, late season; northern Syrah kept fresh acidity and bright fruit, and the vintage drew strong early praise.
A rainy July was followed by wind and sun into September; the northern Rhône whites were excellent, while Syrah was uneven from site to site.
A hot, dry year with heat spikes and drought, balanced by cool nights and late-summer rain, gave rich reds and heady Condrieu.
An early, warm and very dry season with drought stress and small berries; yields were low and the wines concentrated.
A very hot, dry year with a heat spike and a ripe, plentiful crop; the wines were lush and lower in acidity.
A very hot, dry year with heat spikes, drought and hail, but well-timed showers kept freshness, and Côte-Rôtie led the way.
A very dry, early season brought drought and short yields to the northern Rhône, yet the wines turned out fresher than the heat had suggested.
A hot, dry year with a heat spike and drought, eased by August rain, gave fine tannins and good balance.
Storms, hail, mildew, a heat spike and mid-harvest rain made a demanding season, though growers praised the balance of the wines.
A wet spring and cool finish brought mildew and rot pressure; the reds were fresh and early-drinking and the whites particularly successful.
A heat spike, drought and a small crop gave low yields across the northern Rhône; despite the stress, growers judged the quality of the grapes high.

A Labor Day heatwave brought three days near 105°F, then wildfires broke out on the night of 8 October. Most Sonoma Coast and Russian River fruit was already in, but vineyards still unpicked were exposed to smoke.
The Kincade Fire started on 23 October in the Mayacamas east of Alexander Valley; about 92% of Sonoma's grapes had already been picked, and growers rushed in another 3% before evacuations.

The Walbridge and other lightning fires from mid-August and the Glass Fire in late September exposed most of Sonoma's grapes to smoke. Lab results took three to four weeks and some wineries rejected fruit.
An unusually harsh winter freeze cut the crop severely, mostly in reds, to about 34,000 tons; a mild spring and hot summer followed.
Ideal hang time and an even season; for the first time Washington harvested more red than white grapes, about 84,500 tons in all.
Hotter summer highs brought harvest about ten days early, with the first grapes picked on 1 September near Benton City.
A cool start was followed by heat in the mid to high 90s°F; harvest began as early as 9 September and most was in by mid-October.
Late-season heat brought harvest from 2 September on Red Mountain and in Walla Walla; cooler weather from 10 September slowed the pace through late October.
Winter freeze damage hit vineyards in some areas, and the hot season that followed brought an unusually early August start to harvest, which finished in early November.
A mild winter and warm spring gave early, heavy fruit set; a hot summer and cool September and October extended hang time.
A mild, rainy spring and hot, dry summer with a strong day-night shift, then a cool, humid, rainy September and dry, sunny October.
An even spring, warm late spring and uneven summer with heat spikes, then a cool, sunny, dry autumn that allowed long hang time.
A cool, rainy spring delayed budbreak by about two weeks and a cool summer followed; harvest ran 10 to 14 days late in a dry autumn.
A record-hot July rushed ripening, and an early frost on 11 October damaged about 15% of the crop before harvest was complete.
Early April budbreak, then a cool, wet spring and cool summer; a hot spell from late September to late October rescued ripening before cool, wet weather returned.
Late-2010 freeze damage in the Horse Heaven Hills and Walla Walla, then a cool summer, gave a light crop and the latest harvest on record for many vineyards.
A warm, sunny, dry season with ripening on schedule and a large day-night temperature swing, with Walla Walla near 30°F in early September.
A warm spring and summer with warmer nights than usual pushed ripening ahead; a mid-September temperature drop then slowed it and extended harvest into early November, giving about 210,000 tons.
A second straight record-warm year in Washington, with record July and August temperatures in some locations and warmth lasting into mid-October, giving a crop of about 227,000 tons.
The warmest vintage to that date: Columbia Valley averaged about 3,157 growing degree days against a long-term 2,628, Red Mountain topped 3,900, and some wineries picked in mid-August.
Bloom came more than two weeks early and May was on pace for record warmth, before cooler weather from June; Washington harvested a record 270,000 tons.
A cool, wet winter and spring, a late budbreak, a hot July and August and cooling in late September pushed harvest into early November.
A cool April, a May among the warmest on record, a cool June and a hot July and August were followed by a cool September and a long harvest.
Snow in February and March delayed vineyard work, a cool, even summer followed, and statewide frosts in early to mid October left some fruit unpicked.
Wildfire smoke in the second week of September paused picking for about ten days, a freeze on 25 October ended the season, and the crop was well down.
Record heat in late June, the Pacific Northwest heat dome, made the season possibly the warmest on record; sparkling picks began on 12 August, and berries and clusters were small.
A cold, wet winter and an April blizzard stalled budbreak by two to three weeks, so the whole season ran late until a warm late September and October ripened a large crop.
A cool start delayed budbreak by about two weeks, then a warm May, hot June and one August heat spike; the crop was about 34% smaller.
Extreme January cold threatened the vintage and cut the crop to about 150,000 tons; the rest of the season was stress-free.
A sunny, warm summer without excessive heat brought harvest from the third week of August, and a cool late September and October extended hang time; the crop was about 108,000 tons.
A wet spring and warm summer were followed by a harvest soaked by moisture from two hurricanes, Irene and Lee, so rot management was critical.
Temperatures near 80°F in March brought record-early budbreak; a warm summer followed and the harvest was the earliest on record at some estates.
The polar vortex winter brought months of temperatures between minus 7 and minus 18°F. Some vineyards lost 100% of their buds, and the USDA declared 19 Finger Lakes counties a disaster area.
A second harsh winter caused bud and vine damage that cut yields, before a hot, sunny summer and dry autumn ripened the reduced crop.
Record-early budbreak after 80°F days in March and a warm summer led to one of the earliest Finger Lakes harvests on record.
The earliest budbreak on record was followed by a hard frost on 18 May; Cornell estimated 30 to 50% of New York's grape crop was damaged.
Budbreak came a full month early on warm, dry soils, and a temperate summer gave long hang time. Napa harvested about 144,000 tons against a ten-year average of 121,000.
A nearly ideal season with a three-day June heat stretch and late-August rain clouds; a compact harvest ended in mid-October, and total tonnage rose noticeably.
A cold March was followed by early heat spikes and the hottest May on record, which pushed harvest two to three weeks early; a cool August preserved hang time.
Early-April frost and May rain, then a mild summer with warm days and cool nights; late-September warmth sped ripening and condensed the harvest.
Early-March heat spikes were followed by the wettest April on record, then a long, cool summer; September heat finally moved the harvest forward.
Bud break earlier than vintners remembered and June heat spikes led to one of the earliest harvests on record, with a smaller-than-average crop.
Winter rains, a dry March, then record late-season rain delayed bloom and set. A cool summer and an Indian summer extended hang time for a larger-than-average crop.
New Year flooding and a wet spring delayed budbreak, then a record ten-day heatwave in July struck before canopies were thinned; early-October rain fell after the white harvest.
A dry, warm winter brought early budding and bloom; a Labor Day heat spike boosted sugars, then cool weather and a warm Indian summer followed.
The driest spring on record brought the deepest frost in decades, then a heat spike at bloom. Rainfall was about 60% of normal for a second year, and a Labor Day heatwave compressed the harvest.
A frost-free spring after the 2008 frosts and only four or five days above 100°F, against a typical 14; rainfall was about two-thirds of normal, but well-timed rain kept the vines in balance.
Rain returned after three dry years and a cool summer slowed veraison; a two-day heat spike on 24 August sunburned exposed fruit, and the harvest was late, short and small.

A wet winter and June rain at bloom caused shatter, cutting some crops by over 30%. A cool summer gave the latest sparkling-wine start in memory, on 29 August, and mid-October rain brought botrytis to unpicked fruit.
A near-ideal spring and steady flowering, warm days and foggy nights; yields were about 30% above the two previous years, back near normal.
A warm, dry spring with early budbreak and ideal flowering; only one heat spike interrupted optimal temperatures, and ripening was early and even.
A third drought year and the South Napa earthquake of 24 August, yet near-perfect weather; sparkling picks began on 30 July and most of the harvest finished two weeks early.
A warm late winter brought early budbreak, but a cold May bloom caused uneven set and a small crop. Rain was 75% of normal and harvest began on 22 July, among the earliest on record.
An early start and ideal weather through a steady summer and warm late season; the first significant autumn rain arrived only on 14 October.
A Labor Day heatwave sped up picking, and by 8 October, when wind-driven wildfires broke out, nearly 90% of Napa's tonnage was already in. The fruit still hanging faced the smoke.
Abundant February rain, late, even flowering and a marine-cooled summer without major heat spikes gave a long, relaxed season and a crop 20 to 30% larger than usual.
Heavy early rain and late soil moisture, then a long, warm summer with few heat events and foggy mornings; a mild finish extended hang time.

A dry winter, then the LNU Lightning Complex fire from 17 August and the Glass Fire from 27 September filled the valley with smoke. Smoke taint fears meant the red harvest was much smaller than usual.
A second drought year with very little rain gave small berries and low yields; whites were picked from 30 July and reds from 31 August, one of the earliest harvests on record.
Five days of triple-digit heat in early September, during a record heatwave, were followed by rain that halted picking; mild October weather let late reds hang longer.
Full reservoirs after a wet winter and spring, then a mild summer gave above-average yields and one of the longest seasons in a decade, with picking from Labor Day to mid-November.
Heavy winter rain carried vines through a hot summer, and canopies shaded the fruit. The harvest was low-stress but compressed, with still wines picked from mid-August to mid-October.
A cooler season with ample rain and only about eight days above 95°F. Yields came in higher than expected, rain paused crush pads, and mildew pressure rose.
A moderate to warm, even season with light rain toward the end of harvest gave ripe Pinot Noir with moderate acidity.
Ideal flowering led to higher yields, and a warm, dry summer ripened the resulting large crop of Willamette Pinot Noir to full ripeness.
Early budbreak and a moderate summer without heat spikes; an inch of September rain eased water stress, and a warm, dry autumn allowed an extended harvest with full yields.
A hot, dry season in the Willamette Valley produced clean, very ripe fruit, a warm contrast to the cooler Oregon vintages on either side of it.
Poor weather at fruit set meant low yields, then a hot, dry summer with light August and September rain ripened the short Willamette crop.
Early budbreak, then cool weather delayed flowering and fruit set; a warm, dry summer followed, and light September rain fell as the Pinot Noir neared harvest.
Favourable bloom, then a warm, dry summer; heat and wind before harvest caused some dehydration in the grapes, concentrating sugars before picking.
Summer heat spikes, a cool September and successive rainstorms delayed harvest, and birds were a problem for growers waiting on ripeness.
Late budbreak and a moderate summer gave a late season with low yields, but ideal harvest conditions let growers pick fully ripe Pinot Noir.
A warm, dry spring with good flowering and heavy crop loads, then a warm, dry summer that caused some dehydration.
A cool spring and summer followed a mild, dry winter, and a warm October finally helped ripen the grapes for harvest.
Oregon's latest and coldest season on record: flowering came in July, veraison in September and harvest in late October and November, rescued by sunny late-autumn days.
A cool spring with delayed bloom and wet weather hurt fruit set and reduced yields, then a warm, dry summer and dry autumn ripened the short crop.
A warm, early season was cut in two by a heavy late-September rain event, which halted picking; rot and mildew pressure followed in a warm October.
A warm, dry spring with ideal flowering set a large crop, and a warm, dry season through to harvest ripened all of it fully.
Oregon's hottest year on record to that point: an early spring, ideal flowering and a warm, dry summer gave a large crop picked early at high ripeness.
An early year from budbreak to harvest, warm but without the heat of the three previous vintages, with slightly reduced yields.
A rainy winter and wet, cool spring, then late-May heat that set off flowering, plentiful rain and a warm season produced above-average Willamette yields.
A cool spring delayed budburst, then warm weather and drought from May to September gave lower yields with smaller clusters and berries, and ideal harvest conditions.
A wet late winter and spring and near-record June to July rain raised disease pressure; early-September rain complicated picking in a cool season.
After a dry season with mild spring frosts that reduced yields, strong east winds in early September drove wildfire smoke into the valley and caused widespread smoke taint.
One of the driest seasons on record; a cold, wet spell at flowering hurt fruit set, then the late-June heat dome set record temperatures before veraison. The small crop came through clean.
An April frost damaged primary buds and the season started cool, but yields beat 2021 and the warmest October on record ripened the crop.
A warm, dry season with light yields; an August heatwave caused burn and shrivel, so careful sorting and precise picking dates were needed.
A January freeze reduced yields, and heat spikes struck in July and September; a warm, dry September let growers pick at their own pace.
A warm, dry season ripened the Willamette crop early and fast, with small berries and concentrated fruit, though the wines are still too young to judge.
The after-effects of drought, with no post-harvest irrigation and early leaf fall, gave South Africa its smallest crop since 2005, and Stellenbosch was among the worst-hit regions.
One of the smallest crops of the decade: rolling blackouts stopped irrigation, December rain brought mildew and unseasonal March rain stretched harvest into April.
A multiyear drought that brought Cape Town close to running out of water cut South Africa's crop by about 20%, the smallest since 2005; Swartland yields were about 50% down on average.
After late-September 2023 floods and windy spring storms, Swartland had only 35 mm of rain from October to March against 110 to 135 mm in the previous three seasons, and yields were very low.
